claims: A pure Transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches performs very well on image classification tasks, removing the prior reliance on CNNs for vision Transformer applications.

When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks, Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

Prior vision works either applied attention in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used attention to replace certain convolutional components while retaining the overall convolutional network structure.
Vision Transformers dominate ResNets on the performance/compute trade-off, using approximately 2-4× less compute to attain the same performance averaged over 5 datasets.
Hybrid ResNet-ViT models slightly outperform pure ViT at small computational budgets, but this performance difference vanishes for larger models.
Vision Transformers do not show performance saturation within the tested pre-training compute range, motivating future scaling efforts.

The Vision Transformer reshapes input images into flattened 2D patch sequences, maps patches to a constant latent dimension D via trainable linear projection, and prepends a learnable class token whose final encoder state serves as the image representation.

Vision Transformer introduces no image-specific inductive biases into the architecture apart from the initial patch extraction step, processing images as patch sequences via a standard Transformer encoder as used in NLP.
Vision Transformer matches or exceeds the state of the art on many image classification datasets while being relatively cheap to pre-train.

Prior hybrid CNN-Transformer vision models that replaced convolutions entirely have not been scaled effectively on modern hardware accelerators due to use of specialized attention patterns, leaving classic ResNet-like architectures as state of the art for large-scale image recognition prior to this work.
Convolutional architectures remained dominant in computer vision at the time of the study, even as Transformer models scaled to 100B parameters in NLP with no sign of saturating performance.

claim_records.text: The routine of the current ViT model is to maintain a full-length patch sequence during inference, which is redundant and lacks hierarchical representation.

The proposed Hierarchical Visual Transformer (HVT) progressively pools visual tokens to shrink the sequence length and hence reduces the computational cost, analogous to the feature maps downsampling in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).

HVT brings the benefit that model capacity can be increased by scaling dimensions of depth/width/resolution/patch size without introducing extra computational complexity due to the reduced sequence length.
The average pooled visual tokens contain more discriminative information than the single class token.
With comparable FLOPs, HVT outperforms the competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 datasets for the image classification task.

claim_records.text: Vision Transformers' inherent reliance on sequential input enforces the manual partitioning of images into patch sequences, which disrupts the image's inherent structural and semantic continuity.
The proposed Pattern Transformer (Patternformer) adaptively converts images to pattern sequences for Transformer input.

Patternformer employs a Convolutional Neural Network to extract various patterns from the input image, with each channel representing a unique pattern that is fed into the succeeding Transformer as a visual token.
By enabling the network to optimize these patterns, each pattern concentrates on its local region of interest, thereby preserving its intrinsic structural and semantic information.
Only employing the vanilla ResNet and Transformer, Patternformer has accomplished state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

claim_records.text: Only employing the vanilla ResNet and Transformer, Patternformer has achieved competitive results on ImageNet.

claim_records.text: Swin Transformer achieves 87.3 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K image classification.
Swin Transformer achieves 58.7 box AP on COCO test-dev for object detection.
Swin Transformer achieves 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev for object detection.
Swin Transformer achieves 53.5 mIoU on ADE20K val for semantic segmentation.
The shifted windowing scheme in Swin Transformer brings greater efficiency by limiting self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while also allowing for cross-window connection.
The hierarchical Swin Transformer architecture has linear computational complexity with respect to image size.
Existing Transformer-based models use tokens of fixed scale, a property unsuitable for vision applications where visual elements vary substantially in scale.
The computational complexity of standard Transformer self-attention is quadratic to image size, making dense prediction on high-resolution images intractable.

Swin Transformer builds hierarchical feature maps by merging image patches in deeper layers and has linear computation complexity to input image size due to self-attention computation only within each local window.
Previous vision Transformers produce feature maps of a single low resolution and have quadratic computation complexity to input image size due to global self-attention computation.

A Swin Transformer block consists of a shifted window based MSA module, followed by a 2-layer MLP with GELU non-linearity, with LayerNorm applied before each module and residual connections after each module.

Swin Transformer has the same feature map resolutions as typical convolutional networks such as VGG and ResNet, allowing it to conveniently replace existing backbone networks for various vision tasks.
Prior works that compute self-attention within a local window of each pixel achieve slightly better accuracy/FLOPs trade-offs than the counterpart ResNet architecture.

fact_fields.method: Self-attention layers replacing spatial convolution layers in ResNet, with self-attention computed within local window of each pixel

claim_records.text: Prior sliding-window based self-attention layers have costly memory access, causing their actual latency to be significantly larger than that of convolutional networks.

claims: Swin Transformer achieves 87.3 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K image classification.
Swin Transformer achieves 58.7 box AP on COCO test-dev for object detection.
Swin Transformer achieves 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev for object detection.
Swin Transformer achieves 53.5 mIoU on ADE20K val for semantic segmentation.
The shifted windowing scheme in Swin Transformer brings greater efficiency by limiting self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while also allowing for cross-window connection.
The hierarchical Swin Transformer architecture has linear computational complexity with respect to image size.
Existing Transformer-based models use tokens of fixed scale, a property unsuitable for vision applications where visual elements vary substantially in scale.
The computational complexity of standard Transformer self-attention is quadratic to image size, making dense prediction on high-resolution images intractable.

Swin Transformer builds hierarchical feature maps by merging image patches in deeper layers and has linear computation complexity to input image size due to self-attention computation only within each local window.
Previous vision Transformers produce feature maps of a single low resolution and have quadratic computation complexity to input image size due to global self-attention computation.

A Swin Transformer block consists of a shifted window based MSA module, followed by a 2-layer MLP with GELU non-linearity, with LayerNorm applied before each module and residual connections after each module.

Swin Transformer has the same feature map resolutions as typical convolutional networks such as VGG and ResNet, allowing it to conveniently replace existing backbone networks for various vision tasks.
Prior works that compute self-attention within a local window of each pixel achieve slightly better accuracy/FLOPs trade-offs than the counterpart ResNet architecture.
Prior sliding-window based self-attention layers have costly memory access, causing their actual latency to be significantly larger than that of convolutional networks.
Shifting windows between consecutive layers in Swin Transformer allows for a more efficient implementation in general hardware.

claim_records.text: Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) introduces only a small amount (less than 1% of model parameters) of trainable parameters in the input space while keeping the model backbone frozen, as an efficient and effective alternative to full fine-tuning for large-scale Transformer models in vision.
VPT achieves significant performance gains compared to other parameter efficient tuning protocols across extensive experiments on a wide variety of downstream recognition tasks.
VPT outperforms full fine-tuning in many cases across model capacities and training data scales, while reducing per-task storage cost.
ViT-Huge has 632M parameters, which is significantly larger than the 25M parameters of ResNet-50.
VPT-deep enables linearly separable representations while using less parameters than full fine-tuning.
Adding extra tunable parameters for every Transformer layer (VPT-deep) improves performance compared to VPT-shallow, which only inserts prompts for the first layer's input.
On Clevr/count, VPT-deep and full fine-tuning recover the underlying manifold structure of the task, unlike VPT-shallow and Linear.
The ADE20K semantic segmentation task is evaluated with the SETR-PUP Transformer model, which adds a standard ConvNet head to the ViT backbone to perform segmentation.
Full fine-tuning of the pre-trained model requires storing and deploying a separate copy of the backbone parameters for every single task.
All backbones used in the experiment are pre-trained on ImageNet-21k, including Vision Transformers (ViT) and Swin Transformers (Swin).
The Full fine-tuning protocol fully updates all backbone and classification head parameters.
The Linear baseline treats the pre-trained backbone as a feature extractor with fixed weights during tuning, using only a linear layer as the classification head.
VPT works well in the larger ConvNet backbone ConvNeXt-B (pre-trained on ImageNet-21k), offering accuracy gains over other sparse tuning protocols and outperforming Full on 8 out of 19 cases.
The advantages of VPT diminish with the smaller ConvNet ResNet-50 (pre-trained on ImageNet-1k), as there is no clear winner for all 19 VTAB-1k tasks.
The value of p (number of learnable prompt pixels) in the VPT experiment is 2 orders of magnitude smaller than previous work, e.g., 5 vs. 263.

claim_records.text: Depthwise separable convolutions (DSC) make CNNs more efficient in time and memory complexity without deteriorating their accuracy, and sometimes even improving it, as an approximation of regular convolution.
Implementing DSC into the Pretrained Audio Neural Networks (PANN) family for audio classification on AudioSet shows benefits in terms of accuracy/model size trade-off.
The adapted ConvNeXt model rapidly overfits on the audio classification task on AudioSet.
The best ConvNeXt model reached 0.471 mean-average precision on AudioSet, which is better than or equivalent to recent large audio transformers, while using three times less parameters.
The adapted ConvNeXt model achieved positive results in audio captioning and audio retrieval tasks.

claim_records.text: The exploration from a standard ResNet toward vision Transformer design produces a family of pure ConvNet models named ConvNeXt.

fact_fields.method: Gradual modernization of a standard ResNet toward vision Transformer design

claim_records.text: Hierarchical Transformers such as Swin Transformers reintroduced several ConvNet priors, making Transformers practically viable as a generic vision backbone.
Vision Transformers quickly superseded ConvNets as the state-of-the-art image classification model after the start of the Roaring 20s of visual recognition.
ViT introduces no image-specific inductive bias and makes minimal changes to the original NLP Transformers, except for the initial patchify layer that splits an image into a sequence of patches.
With larger model and dataset sizes, Transformers can outperform standard ResNets by a significant margin on image classification tasks.
ViT's global attention design has quadratic complexity with respect to input size, which is acceptable for ImageNet classification but quickly becomes intractable with higher-resolution inputs.

The exploration considers two model sizes in terms of FLOPs: one around 4.5×10^9 FLOPs corresponding to ResNet-50 / Swin-T regime, and another around 15.0×10^9 FLOPs corresponding to ResNet-200 / Swin-B regime.

fact_fields.method: Roadmap exploration from ResNet to a ConvNet resembling Transformers

claim_records.text: ConvNeXt achieves ImageNet-1K classification accuracy significantly exceeding Swin-T's 81.3% in the ResNet-50 / Swin-T compute regime.

ConvNeXt has approximately the same FLOPs, parameter count, throughput, and memory use as the Swin Transformer, but does not require specialized modules such as shifted window attention or relative position biases.

For ResNet-200 regime experiments, changing the stage block ratio from (3, 24, 36, 3) to Swin-B's (3, 3, 27, 3) drastically reduces FLOPs, so width is increased from 64 to 84 to keep FLOPs at a similar level.
Inverting dimensions brings a larger improvement at the ResNet-200 regime than at the ResNet-50 regime, with +0.79% versus +0.14%.

fact_fields.method: Dimension inversion step in modernization roadmap

claim_records.text: After adopting depthwise convolutions in the ResNet-200 regime, width is further increased to 128, matching Swin-B's width.

claim_records.text: The reference convolution-free DeiT vision transformer with 86M parameters achieves 83.1% top-1 accuracy under single-crop evaluation on ImageNet, with no external training data.
DeiT models can be trained on a single computer in less than 3 days.
When using the proposed token-based distillation strategy, DeiT achieves up to 85.2% accuracy on ImageNet.
The DeiT-S and DeiT-Ti models are trained on a single node with 4 GPUs in three days, with parameter counts comparable to ResNet-50 and ResNet-18 respectively.
The proposed transformer-specific distillation strategy outperforms vanilla distillation by a significant margin.
With the proposed distillation approach, image transformers learn more from a convnet teacher than from another transformer with comparable performance.
DeiT achieves a 6.3% top-1 accuracy improvement over previous ViT models trained on ImageNet-1k only in a comparable setting.
DeiT⚗, produced via distillation from a relatively weaker RegNetY, outperforms the EfficientNet convnet on ImageNet.

HTR-ConvText introduces the ConvText encoder, a hybrid architecture combining global context and local features within a hierarchical structure that reduces sequence length for improved efficiency.
HTR-ConvText includes an auxiliary module that injects textual context to mitigate the weakness of Connectionist Temporal Classification.

claim_records.text: ViT achieves inferior performance to CNNs when trained from scratch on a midsize dataset like ImageNet.
The simple tokenization of input images in ViT fails to model important local structure such as edges and lines among neighboring pixels, leading to low training sample efficiency.
The redundant attention backbone design of ViT leads to limited feature richness for fixed computation budgets and limited training samples.

T2T-ViT incorporates a layer-wise Tokens-to-Token (T2T) transformation that progressively structurizes the image to tokens by recursively aggregating neighboring Tokens into one Token, such that local structure represented by surrounding tokens can be modeled and tokens length can be reduced.
T2T-ViT reduces the parameter count and MACs of vanilla ViT by half, while achieving more than 3.0% improvement when trained from scratch on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT outperforms ResNets and achieves comparable performance with MobileNets by directly training on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT with comparable size to ResNet50 (21.5M parameters) achieves 83.3% top1 accuracy at image resolution 384×384 on ImageNet.
T2T-ViT-14, T2T-ViT-19 and T2T-ViT-24 are designed to have comparable parameters with ResNet50, ResNet101 and ResNet152 respectively.

T2T-ViT-7 and T2T-ViT-12 are lite models with comparable model size to MobileNetV1 and MobileNetV2, with no special efficient convolution designs and only reduced layer depth, hidden dimension, and MLP ratio.

Five architecture designs borrowed from CNNs were explored for ViT backbone: Dense connection as DenseNet, deep-narrow vs. shallow-wide structure as in Wide-ResNets, channel attention as Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks, more split heads in multi-head attention layer as ResNeXt, and Ghost operations as GhostNet.

# Original ViT Against CNN Backbones: A Mechanism, Data-Scale, and Task-Fit Comparison

## Abstract

The original Vision Transformer is a convolution-free, single-scale patch-sequence model whose strongest evidence is conditional: after large-scale pretraining, it transferred strongly to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and related recognition benchmarks relative to state-of-the-art CNNs, with a favorable training-compute claim in that study. ResNet-like CNNs instead encode locality, weight sharing and staged multi-resolution features by construction. The review therefore separates architecture from pretraining and downstream task: plain ViT offers early global, content-dependent token mixing, while CNN backbones provide stronger built-in visual priors and natural feature pyramids for detection and segmentation. Later PVT, Swin, CvT, HVT and ViT-CoMer results show the value of hierarchy, windows, pooling or convolution, but do not measure the unmodified ViT. Broad benchmarks and CLIP studies further show that task, data scale, model size and objective can change the comparison. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:section:abstract:2:597bb93edd49:claim:fd1eb0c7fdbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:27c2098d37c4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:364b11f79c92] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:11:8c6502676046:claim:2639c62fb151] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:11:9ac4f7bb3c0b:claim:2bed41577ceb] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:0:25667294cdf8:claim:5a15057132a5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:ab2334242752] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:a57dcb4dfff3] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:f6e0fad53ed7] [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3] [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:06141737f41f]

## Introduction

This review compares the original Vision Transformer, introduced as a convolution-free model that treats an image as a sequence of fixed-size patches and applies a standard Transformer encoder, with convolutional neural-network backbones such as ResNet-like and later ConvNeXt models. The organizing choice is to separate architecture from training recipe and downstream use: inductive bias and feature aggregation, dependence on pretraining scale, ImageNet classification evidence, and suitability as a backbone for detection or segmentation. This is a review grouping rather than a universal taxonomy, and later hybrid or hierarchical Transformers are used only where they clarify a limitation of the original ViT. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:section:abstract:2:597bb93edd49:claim:fd1eb0c7fdbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] At the time ViT appeared, convolutional architectures dominated large-scale visual recognition. ViT's central claim was not that attention universally beats convolution under every setting, but that reliance on CNNs was unnecessary: when pretrained on sufficiently large data and transferred to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks, the pure patch-Transformer achieved strong results relative to state-of-the-art CNNs while using substantially fewer computational resources to train. That qualification matters because the same paper positioned classic ResNet-like CNNs as the large-scale image-recognition baseline to beat. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:section:abstract:2:597bb93edd49:claim:fd1eb0c7fdbc]

The comparison cannot be reduced to one ImageNet accuracy number. Broad backbone benchmarks show that architecture, pretraining algorithm, pretraining dataset size, and target task interact: Battle of the Backbones evaluated more than 1,500 runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks, and reported that supervised convolutional models were strongest on most tasks among the models considered, while also finding that ViTs were more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. CLIP-focused comparisons likewise report that ViT and ConvNet backbones can differ substantially in classifications, calibration, invariance and transfer behavior even when trained with the same objective and at comparable accuracy or compute. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5] [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3]

The scope therefore distinguishes the original ViT from later designs that add CNN-like hierarchy, windows, convolutions, pyramids, or dense-prediction adapters. Evidence from PVT, Swin, CvT and ViT-CoMer is relevant because it identifies what the original plain ViT lacked for pixel-level tasks—multi-resolution feature maps, local interactions, and efficient high-resolution processing—but it should not be read as evidence that the original ViT itself possessed those backbone properties. The remaining sections examine these distinctions, compare matched experimental evidence where available, and leave settings with different pretraining, architecture or task pipelines explicitly non-comparable. ## Background and Method Taxonomy

Classification criteria for this comparison. This review groups backbones by four separable dimensions rather than treating “ViT” and “CNN” as single immutable classes: (1) the basic spatial operator—fixed learned convolution kernels versus content-dependent self-attention over patch tokens; (2) the spatial and scale structure—single-resolution token grids versus staged, downsampled feature pyramids; (3) the visual inductive bias—locality, weight sharing and hierarchical processing built into CNNs versus the weaker spatial priors of plain ViT; and (4) the deployment context—classification from a global representation versus dense tasks that consume multi-scale feature maps. These are comparison axes for this chapter, not a paper-defined universal taxonomy, and a model can be hybrid on more than one axis. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe]

The first axis separates the original plain ViT from conventional CNN backbones without conflating it with later Transformer variants. ViT enters an image as non-overlapping patch embeddings and processes the resulting sequence with standard Transformer self-attention and residual blocks; CNN backbones apply shared convolutional kernels over local neighborhoods and typically stack stages with changing resolution and channel width. A CNN’s locality and translation-equivariant weight sharing are architectural priors, whereas ViT must learn more of its spatial organization from data. This distinction does not imply that attention and convolution are mathematically unrelated: later work interprets vision Transformers as input-conditioned, dynamic convolutions, but that unifying analysis is a design lens rather than evidence that the original ViT has the same feature hierarchy as a ResNet. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:bd0e5c2f2892]

The second axis is especially important for backbone use. A conventional CNN backbone such as ResNet naturally produces staged feature maps at progressively lower spatial resolution; PVT explicitly follows this convention by producing pyramid features at strides 4, 8, 16 and 32, using patch-embedding stages rather than convolutional strides. Swin likewise adopts resolutions comparable to VGG- and ResNet-like networks so it can replace CNN backbones in existing vision pipelines. The original ViT is not in this staged-pyramid class: its plain patch grid primarily supports global classification, which is why later dense-prediction systems add pyramids, windows, adapters, or convolutional features. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:43e71b72c083]

The third axis distinguishes architecture from training recipe. A model family can be a ViT, ConvNet, or hybrid independently of whether its weights were initialized randomly, supervised on ImageNet-1K or ImageNet-21K, self-supervised with methods such as DINO or MAE, or trained with CLIP. Battle of the Backbones treats pretraining method, dataset scale and architecture as separate benchmark variables, and reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and model size. Therefore, a result obtained by a CLIP ViT, a self-supervised ViT, or a ViT using advanced external pretraining cannot be assigned to the original supervised-from-scratch ViT mechanism without matching those conditions. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5] [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3]

The fourth axis separates image classification from dense prediction and other backbone objectives. Classification mainly asks for a global image label and can use a class token or pooled representation; object detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation require spatially localized, often multi-scale features. PVT motivates its pyramid Transformer as a direct CNN-backbone replacement for pixel-level tasks, while ViT-CoMer states that plain ViT is weak in dense prediction because of limited inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. These task-fit criteria are different from lightweight-model objectives such as reducing parameters, FLOPs, throughput or edge latency: efficiency may affect whether a backbone is practical, but it does not by itself establish the required feature structure. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:364b11f79c92] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:0:25667294cdf8:claim:5a15057132a5] [E:arxiv:2505.03113:abstract:claim:031cda985d75]

Under these axes, the relevant family relationships are: original ViT is a plain, convolution-free, single-scale sequence model; ResNet-like CNNs are local, hierarchical, multi-stage backbones; PVT and Swin are vision-specific Transformers that introduce CNN-like pyramids or windowed hierarchy; CvT is a hybrid that introduces convolutional token embedding and convolutional projections into Transformer blocks; and ViT-CoMer is an adapted plain-ViT backbone that injects convolutional multi-scale features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion. These later models are comparators and evidence for trade-offs, not restatements of the original ViT. Conversely, comparisons of CLIP, OOD behavior, calibration or invariance characterize representations under particular training and evaluation protocols; they should not be collapsed into an architecture-only ranking. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55] [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3]

## Representative Methods

Original ViT mechanism. The original Vision Transformer removes convolution from the image-recognition backbone rather than merely inserting attention into a ResNet. Its input pipeline divides an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embeds each patch, adds positional information, and feeds the resulting token sequence—together with a class token in the standard formulation—into a standard Transformer encoder. The encoder blocks use multi-head self-attention, MLPs, normalization and residual connections. The contribution was to show that a pure sequence model applied directly to image patches could perform very well on image classification, but the paper's evidence was conditional on large-scale pretraining followed by transfer to mid-sized or smaller recognition benchmarks; it did not establish that the same architecture is data-efficient or dense-prediction ready when trained from limited data. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:section:abstract:2:597bb93edd49:claim:fd1eb0c7fdbc]

ViT's aggregation differs from a CNN at the level of the spatial operator. In self-attention, each patch token can attend to every other token in the same layer, so global context can be aggregated early rather than being reached only after stacking many local convolutional layers. This content-dependent, all-to-all routing is the main mechanism behind ViT's long-range modeling. CKA-based analysis of ViTs and ResNets finds a corresponding internal difference: ViT representations are more uniform across layers, lower and higher ViT layers are more similar to one another, and self-attention enables early global aggregation. The same analysis attributes strong propagation from lower to higher layers partly to ViT residual connections. These findings describe learned representations on image-classification analyses; they do not by themselves show that global attention is more accurate or cheaper than convolution under every training setup. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6bd2853bda8d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7ba124bd8379] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6034e1cc45df] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:edef6a17e795]

ViT's weak visual priors define both its opportunity and its boundary. Unlike CNNs, the plain model does not build locality, translation-equivariant weight sharing, or a staged multi-resolution feature pyramid into the backbone. With enough pretraining data, this reduced inductive bias can permit flexible learning and strong transfer, which is the premise of the original ViT result. With smaller datasets, however, CvT reports that vision Transformers remain below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets and identifies the strong two-dimensional local structure of natural images as a reason convolutional properties can help. Thus, the relevant contrast is not “global reasoning versus no global reasoning” alone: CNNs encode local visual structure efficiently, while ViT relies more heavily on data to learn relationships that convolution already assumes. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6]

CNN backbone mechanism. Convolutional backbones apply learned kernels over local neighborhoods and share those kernels across spatial positions. This supplies translation-equivariant feature extraction and a local receptive field that grows as layers are composed. The CNN backbone lineage cited around ViT includes stacked convolutional blocks and ResNet-like architectures that were dominant in large-scale image recognition at the time; later backbone comparisons also use modern ConvNeXt models. A typical CNN backbone is organized into stages that downsample feature maps and increase channel width, producing hierarchical features suitable both for a final classifier and for detection or segmentation heads. The mechanism is therefore local, weight-shared, and hierarchical by construction rather than a single global sequence operation. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:section:abstract:2:597bb93edd49:claim:fd1eb0c7fdbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5]

ResNet-like CNNs should not be characterized as models that cannot capture long-range information. A single convolution is local, but repeated convolutional stages, residual blocks and downsampling expand the effective receptive field and compose local evidence into increasingly abstract features. Their advantage is that this composition comes with strong image-specific priors and hardware-mature dense operators. Their limitation relative to plain ViT is that direct interaction between distant image regions is not available in one attention-like operation; it must arise through the network's depth and receptive-field growth. This is an architectural comparison of mechanisms, not a claim that a particular CNN is always less accurate: matched training data, model size, resolution and augmentation determine the measured outcome. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8]

Evidence and applicability of the original ViT. ViT's strongest supported application in its original paper is transfer learning for image classification after large-scale pretraining. The paper reports that pretraining on large data and transferring to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and related benchmarks yields excellent results compared with state-of-the-art convolutional networks, while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. The applicable boundary is embedded in that result: ViT is a pure patch-sequence classifier whose success depends on access to sufficiently large pretraining data. It should not be treated as a direct plug-in multi-scale detector backbone merely because it obtains strong classification accuracy. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68]

Representation analyses reinforce that ViT and CNNs solve classification with measurably different internal structures. On image-classification benchmarks, ViTs preserve more uniform similarity across layers and retain spatial information, while ResNets show more separation between lower and higher stages. Cross-model CKA comparisons indicate that many lower ResNet layers correspond roughly to the lowest portion of ViT layers, and that the final portion of ViT layers is less similar to ResNet representations. These results support a mechanism-level distinction—early global mixing and strong residual feature propagation in ViT versus stage-wise convolutional abstraction—but they are analyses of representation similarity and spatial localization, not a substitute for matched top-1 accuracy, detection AP, or segmentation mIoU comparisons. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6bd2853bda8d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7ba124bd8379] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:edef6a17e795]

PVT shows what must be added to use a Transformer as a general CNN-style dense-prediction backbone. Rather than retaining a single plain token resolution, PVT builds a four-stage feature pyramid with output strides of 4, 8, 16 and 32. It uses progressive patch embedding to shrink the sequence and constructs feature maps that can feed classification, detection and segmentation pipelines. Its stated goal is to be a convolution-free alternative that can directly replace CNN backbones for pixel-level tasks. PVT is therefore not the original ViT mechanism: it borrows the hierarchical backbone convention used by CNNs and demonstrates that pyramid structure, not self-attention alone, is central to its dense-task applicability. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:27c2098d37c4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:364b11f79c92]

Swin Transformer addresses a different plain-ViT limitation through hierarchical, window-local attention. Its blocks replace the standard multi-head self-attention module with window-based and shifted-window self-attention, while retaining LayerNorm, MLPs and residual connections; the network is built in stages with patch merging and feature-map resolutions comparable to VGG or ResNet. The stated purpose of matching typical convolutional-network resolutions is to allow Swin to replace CNN backbones in existing vision methods. Swin's shifted windows provide cross-window connection while avoiding global attention over every token, but this is a vision-specific redesign rather than the original ViT's global patch-to-patch attention. Its evidence supports the utility of local windows and hierarchy, not an assertion that original ViT already had those properties. [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:11:8c6502676046:claim:2639c62fb151]

CvT is a hybrid mechanism that moves in the opposite direction from ViT's convolution-free design. It introduces a convolutional token embedding and convolutional projections inside a hierarchical Transformer, intending to combine CNN properties such as locality and shift, scale and distortion robustness with Transformer properties such as dynamic attention, global context and generalization. CvT also reports that its design removes the need for explicit positional encoding. Its contribution is evidence that convolution can improve ViT-oriented performance and efficiency, but the resulting model is not the original ViT: it deliberately changes tokenization, attention projection and scale structure. Consequently, CvT results cannot be used as a direct measurement of plain ViT versus ResNet unless the plain ViT and CNN baselines are separately reported under matched settings. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:11:9ac4f7bb3c0b:claim:2bed41577ceb]

ViT-CoMer clarifies the dense-prediction boundary of plain ViT from the adapter side. Its authors state that ViT underperforms in dense prediction because it lacks inner-patch information interaction and has limited feature-scale diversity. Their design injects spatial-pyramid, multi-receptive-field convolutional features into ViT and uses bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion to create hierarchical, multi-scale features. The paper frames this as enhancing a plain ViT backbone for object detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation. The mechanism is therefore complementary evidence: convolutional local and pyramid features are added because the plain ViT representation is not naturally organized like a CNN feature pyramid. ViT-CoMer's strong downstream results apply to the adapted model and its pretraining choices, not retroactively to the original ViT. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:0:25667294cdf8:claim:5a15057132a5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:ab2334242752] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:a57dcb4dfff3]

Hierarchical pooling Transformers such as HVT provide another bridge between the two families. HVT progressively pools visual tokens to reduce sequence length, explicitly analogizing this operation to feature-map downsampling in CNNs, and reports that average-pooled tokens can contain more discriminative information than a single class token in its experiments. This design targets the plain-ViT issues of maintaining a full-length sequence and lacking hierarchical representation. It is useful for understanding the mechanism trade-off—token reduction can lower attention cost and permit scaling—but it is a modified Transformer rather than the original model. Its ImageNet and CIFAR-100 results should be read as evidence for hierarchical pooling under that paper's settings, not as a universal ViT–CNN ranking. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:f6e0fad53ed7]

The unified dynamic-convolution view should be distinguished from architectural equivalence. One line of work interprets vision Transformers as ConvNets with input-dependent dynamic convolutions, allowing Transformer and dynamic-Conv design choices to be compared in a common framework. That interpretation can guide new designs—for example, replacing softmax with ConvNet-style components or constructing a depth-wise vision Transformer—but it does not erase the operational differences between a plain ViT and a conventional ResNet. Standard CNNs use fixed, spatially shared kernels over local neighborhoods, whereas ViT attention computes token-dependent interactions over the sequence. The unifying lens is therefore a theoretical and design relationship; it does not make ViT hierarchical, convolutional, or automatically suitable as a dense-prediction backbone. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:bd0e5c2f2892] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:c0f865b71d34]

Training recipe is part of method applicability. The architecture must be separated from whether weights are random, supervised on ImageNet-1K or ImageNet-21K, self-supervised, or trained with CLIP. Battle of the Backbones explicitly benchmarks diverse architectures and pretraining protocols across many tasks and reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and the number of parameters. It also reports that, among the models it considered, supervised convolutional backbones performed best on most tasks, while apples-to-apples comparisons at similar pretraining scale changed conclusions about self-supervised learning. Therefore, a CLIP ViT, DINO ViT, MAE ViT, or ViT-CoMer using advanced pretraining is not methodologically interchangeable with the original ViT's large-scale supervised-transfer setup. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5]

CLIP and other representation-learning studies further demonstrate that architecture and objective interact. Comparisons of ConvNet and ViT backbones trained with CLIP report substantial disparities in classifications even when the same data and objective are used, and note effects from representation normalization, prediction complementarity, calibration, transferability and feature invariance. These findings mean that “ViT versus CNN” cannot be inferred from architecture alone when the two backbones have different training paradigms. They also caution against generalizing the original ViT's supervised image-classification evidence to multimodal pretraining: CLIP ViTs and CLIP ConvNets are distinct instantiations with their own measured behaviors and applicability conditions. [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3] [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:06141737f41f]

Efficiency is a separate method dimension from feature structure. Plain global self-attention has quadratic computational complexity with respect to input resolution in the characterization used by later Transformer analyses, which makes high-resolution dense prediction expensive; surveys of lightweight ViTs likewise identify computation, memory and inference-latency challenges. CNNs tend to use local, hierarchical operators that have been highly optimized for vision hardware, while ViT's theoretical global connectivity can impose substantial attention and memory costs in practice. However, parameters, FLOPs, throughput and latency are not interchangeable: Swin-related work notes that costly memory access can make attention patterns slower in actual latency than convolutional networks even when theoretical trade-offs look favorable. Efficiency claims therefore require the specific resolution, hardware, batch size and implementation. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:c0f865b71d34] [E:arxiv:2505.03113:abstract:claim:031cda985d75] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:11:8c6502676046:claim:2639c62fb151] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:a0fd92373ce7]

Applicability summary by method. The original ViT is best understood as a plain, globally attentive, single-scale classification Transformer whose landmark contribution is showing CNNs are unnecessary when large-data pretraining is available. ResNet-like CNNs are local, hierarchical backbones with stronger built-in visual priors and natural multi-stage feature maps. PVT and Swin adapt Transformer processing toward CNN-style pyramids and staged or local attention; CvT inserts convolution into Transformer tokenization and projection; HVT adds progressive pooling; and ViT-CoMer adds convolutional multi-scale features to make a plain ViT more suitable for dense prediction. These later systems demonstrate convergence around hierarchy and local or multi-scale structure, but their results must be attributed to their modified architectures and training conditions rather than pooled into a single claim about the original ViT. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:f6e0fad53ed7] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55]

The method-level conclusion is therefore conditional rather than monolithic. ViT contributes direct global token mixing and a reduced reliance on hand-built visual priors, with strong evidence under large-scale pretraining and classification transfer. CNN backbones contribute locality, weight sharing, staged abstraction and immediate compatibility with dense-prediction feature hierarchies, often with more favorable data requirements and practical efficiency. Hybrid and vision-specific Transformers do not invalidate either premise; they show that high-performance vision systems can combine global attention with convolution-like locality, hierarchy and scale handling. Any stronger preference requires matched experiments on the same dataset, pretraining corpus, model capacity, resolution, task head and evaluation metric. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

Experimental comparison rule. The strongest comparison is between the original ViT and CNNs only when the dataset, pretraining corpus, model capacity, resolution, task head and metric are matched. The original ViT paper's central experimental claim is a large-scale pretraining-and-transfer result: a pure Transformer over image patches attained excellent results on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and related recognition benchmarks relative to state-of-the-art convolutional networks, while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. This supports ViT as a strong classification model under large-data transfer; it does not support a blanket ranking over CNNs trained from scratch or over CNN backbones used with detection and segmentation heads. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68]

The data-scale qualifier is the main interpretive boundary in the original ViT evidence. The paper was motivated by the continued dominance of classic ResNet-like convolutional architectures in large-scale image recognition and by earlier attention models that had not scaled effectively on modern accelerators. ViT's favorable comparison therefore belongs to a setting where large pretraining supplies the visual structure that CNNs encode architecturally. Later CvT explicitly states that, despite vision-Transformer success at large scale, performance remains below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets when training data are smaller. A small-data ViT result and a large-data ViT transfer result are thus not interchangeable evidence. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:section:abstract:2:597bb93edd49:claim:fd1eb0c7fdbc] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8]

Classification versus CNN baselines should also be read at the level of training regime rather than as a single architecture scorecard. The original paper compares transferred ViT against state-of-the-art convolutional networks across multiple mid-sized or small image-recognition datasets after large-scale pretraining; its reported advantage is in that transfer setting and includes a training-compute claim. By contrast, CvT's matched-family discussion reports a deficit for vision Transformers relative to similarly sized CNNs under smaller-data training, then modifies the Transformer with convolutional token embedding and convolutional projections. These findings are compatible because they test different conditions; they should not be merged into a statement that ViT is universally more accurate than ResNet or vice versa. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6]

Representation experiments reveal a mechanism-level difference that accuracy alone does not show. In CKA analyses of ViTs and ResNets on image-classification benchmarks, ViTs had a more uniform layer-similarity structure, lower and higher ViT layers were more similar than corresponding lower and higher ResNet layers, and ResNet representations separated more clearly into lower and higher stages. Cross-model CKA indicated that the lower half of a 60-layer ResNet was broadly similar to about the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the upper half of ResNet to roughly the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT layers was less similar to ResNet. These are representation-similarity findings, not top-1 accuracy rankings. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6bd2853bda8d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7ba124bd8379] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:edef6a17e795]

The same analysis links those representation differences to the two architectures' operations. Self-attention enables early aggregation of global information, whereas a CNN builds increasingly global representations through stacked local layers, and ViT residual connections strongly propagate lower-layer features into higher layers. The paper also reports that ViTs preserve input spatial information during classification, with effects from the classification method. Thus, the experiments support the conclusion that ViT and ResNet can learn structurally different representations even when both solve image classification; they do not establish that one representation is preferable without specifying the target task and pretraining setup. Dense-prediction experiments expose the most important backbone mismatch. The original ViT is a plain single-scale token classifier, whereas CNN backbones naturally provide staged feature maps for detection and segmentation. PVT directly tests a convolution-free Transformer redesigned as a CNN-style backbone: with a comparable number of parameters, PVT-Large plus RetinaNet achieved 40.4 AP on COCO, surpassing ResNet-50 plus RetinaNet at 36.3 AP by 4.1 absolute AP. The paper also reports PVT-Large at 42.6 AP, 1.6 points above ResNeXt101-64x4d, while using 30% fewer parameters. These results support a pyramid Transformer backbone, not the unmodified original ViT. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:364b11f79c92] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:27c2098d37c4] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:9:567aa3b25c19:claim:8772821c75ce] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79]

The PVT comparison is informative precisely because the architecture changed to satisfy the backbone interface. PVT constructs four feature maps with strides of 4, 8, 16 and 32 using progressive patch embedding, whereas a CNN obtains multi-scale maps through convolutional strides. The COCO RetinaNet comparison therefore says that a hierarchical Transformer can compete with ResNet or ResNeXt backbones under that detector setup. It does not demonstrate that the original ViT's single class-token or single-grid representation would achieve the same AP; the pyramid is part of the method being evaluated. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:be13fb5de3ba:claim:364b11f79c92]

ViT-CoMer supplies a second, later dense-prediction data point from the opposite direction: it retains a plain-ViT core but adds convolutional multi-receptive-field features and CNN–Transformer fusion because the authors identify limited inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity as plain-ViT weaknesses. In its Mask R-CNN plot on COCO val2017, plain ViT-S is listed at 44M parameters and 44.0 box AP, ViT-B at 114M and 45.8 AP, and ViT-L with advanced pretraining at 338M and 48.3 AP. ViT-CoMer-S is 50M and 47.1 AP, ViT-CoMer-B is 129M and 50.2 AP, and with advanced pretraining ViT-CoMer-S reaches 52.1 AP, ViT-CoMer-B 54.2 AP, and ViT-CoMer-L 55.9 AP. These are same-figure comparisons, but the adapted model changes architecture and sometimes pretraining, so they measure enhancement of ViT rather than original ViT versus a CNN under identical capacity. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:43e71b72c083] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:0:25667294cdf8:claim:5a15057132a5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55]

The ViT-CoMer paper also reports stronger headline results with a different detector or configuration than the Mask R-CNN plot: ViT-CoMer-L with advanced pretraining achieved 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 without extra detection data such as Objects365, and 62.1% mIoU on ADE20K validation. Those numbers should not be compared directly with the 55.9 AP Mask R-CNN entry or with PVT-RetinaNet because the task heads and configurations differ. They support the adapted model's dense-prediction capability under the paper's stated advanced-pretraining condition, but they are not an original-ViT result and do not create a fair ranking over CNN backbones absent matched heads and training data. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:0:25667294cdf8:claim:5a15057132a5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:ab2334242752] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:a57dcb4dfff3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:43e71b72c083]

Broad backbone benchmarks reinforce that no single architecture wins every task. Battle of the Backbones ran more than 1,500 training comparisons across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks, including ViT, ResNet, ConvNeXt, Swin and other pretrained backbones. Among the models and settings considered, it reports that supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks, names supervised ConvNeXt-Base, supervised ImageNet-21k SwinV2-Base and CLIP ViT-Base as top models across the suite, and finds ViTs more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. Because architecture, pretraining method and dataset scale vary across the field, this is a benchmark-level pattern, not a controlled refutation of the original ViT's large-scale transfer claim. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5]

CLIP-controlled comparisons add another non-ImageNet dimension. When ConvNet and ViT backbones are trained with the same CLIP data and objective, studies still report substantial disparities in their classifications, effects from normalizing representations, differences in calibration, transferability, feature invariance and types of mistakes, and complementarity between backbone predictions. These experiments show that comparable ImageNet accuracy or compute does not imply equivalent model behavior. They compare CLIP-trained representations, however, and therefore cannot be read as direct evidence about the original ViT's supervised large-scale pretraining protocol or about randomly initialized CNNs. [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3] [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:06141737f41f]

Efficiency comparisons require matched units and must not be inferred from architecture alone. The original ViT paper claims substantially fewer computational resources to train under its large-scale transfer experiments, while later lightweight-ViT surveys identify high computation, memory and inference-latency burdens, especially because global attention scales quadratically with input resolution in the standard characterization. PVT and Swin address sequence and window structure to make Transformer backbones more practical, and Swin-related discussion notes that attention memory access can produce larger actual latency than convolutional networks even when theoretical accuracy/FLOPs trade-offs look favorable. Parameters, FLOPs, throughput and wall-clock latency are different metrics; without matched resolution, hardware, batch size and implementation, these results are not a universal efficiency ranking. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2505.03113:abstract:claim:031cda985d75] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:c0f865b71d34] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:11:8c6502676046:claim:2639c62fb151] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79]

Hybrid results should be attributed to the hybrid intervention. CvT reports that convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection improve ViT performance and efficiency, and that ImageNet-22k-pretrained CvT-W24 reached 87.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k validation; this is evidence for a convolutionalized hierarchical Transformer under its training recipe. HVT reports that progressive token pooling, analogous to CNN downsampling, lets it outperform competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 at comparable FLOPs. Neither number measures the original ViT against a CNN without the added hierarchy or convolution, so they should be treated as evidence that CNN-like structure can improve Transformer designs, not as a head-to-head plain-ViT victory or defeat. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:f6e0fad53ed7] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8]

Overall experimental verdict. The matched original-ViT evidence supports a conditional classification result: with large-scale pretraining and transfer, the plain patch Transformer matched or exceeded strong CNN baselines on several recognition benchmarks and did so with a favorable training-compute claim in that study. CNN backbones retain stronger built-in locality and hierarchy and are the natural comparison point when data are limited or when the target is dense prediction. PVT, Swin, CvT, HVT and ViT-CoMer show that adding pyramid, pooling, windowing or convolutional mechanisms can close or reverse task-specific disadvantages, but their results are not attributable to the original ViT. Across broad modern benchmarks and CLIP analyses, task, pretraining scale, model size and metric change the ordering; therefore the defensible conclusion is conditional complementarity, not a universal winner. ## Limitations and Open Problems

Data dependence remains the central open problem for interpreting the original ViT–CNN comparison. ViT's landmark result is conditional on large-scale pretraining and transfer rather than on architecture alone: the paper demonstrates that a pure patch Transformer can match or exceed strong convolutional networks when enough pretraining data are available, while CvT explicitly reports that vision Transformers remain below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets when trained on smaller data. Battle of the Backbones later finds ViTs more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count across its broad suite. The practical implication is that a practitioner cannot infer ViT's expected benefit from ImageNet-scale or JFT-scale results alone; the relevant pretraining corpus, labels or self-supervised objective, model size and downstream dataset must be matched before claiming an architecture advantage. This is a source-supported limitation of the evidence, not a claim that ViT cannot learn efficiently under any improved recipe. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5]

The original ViT's weak image-specific inductive bias is both a flexibility source and a failure mode. CNNs build locality and translation-equivariant weight sharing into their kernels, whereas plain ViT starts from patch tokens and must learn much of the spatial organization from data. CvT motivates convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection by pointing to the strong two-dimensional local structure of natural images and the small-data disadvantage of Transformers. The unresolved issue is how to obtain ViT's global, content-dependent mixing without paying the full data cost of learning local visual regularities. Hybrid designs show that convolution can help, but they also change the architecture; they do not answer whether the original plain ViT can retain the same behavior with less data under a matched but otherwise unchanged training pipeline. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68]

Dense prediction exposes a structural backbone limitation rather than merely a tuning problem. The original ViT maintains a plain patch-token representation for classification and does not provide the staged, multi-resolution feature maps that CNN backbones expose naturally for detection and segmentation. PVT addresses this by constructing feature maps at strides 4, 8, 16 and 32, and Swin adopts VGG- or ResNet-like feature resolutions so it can replace CNN backbones in existing vision pipelines. ViT-CoMer states the plain-ViT problem more directly as limited inner-patch interaction and limited feature-scale diversity, then adds convolutional pyramid features and bidirectional fusion. The implication is that strong classification transfer does not certify a model as a general vision backbone; high-resolution localization requires an interface and feature hierarchy that the original ViT did not define. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:0:25667294cdf8:claim:5a15057132a5] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55]

High-resolution efficiency remains unresolved because global self-attention couples every token to every other token. Later analyses characterize vanilla ViT attention as quadratic in input resolution, and lightweight-ViT surveys identify computation, memory and inference-latency burdens that limit real-world use. This matters more for detection and segmentation than for 224×224 classification because increasing image resolution rapidly increases the token count. PVT reduces the sequence through progressive shrinking, Swin restricts attention to windows and shifts windows across blocks, and HVT pools tokens in a manner analogous to CNN downsampling. These are evidence-supported responses, but they alter global mixing or feature structure; the original ViT's unrestricted early global interaction and efficient high-resolution deployment therefore remain in tension. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:4:61025eb4437f:claim:c0f865b71d34] [E:arxiv:2505.03113:abstract:claim:031cda985d75] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:f6e0fad53ed7]

Theoretical compute is also not sufficient for deployment decisions. Swin-related discussion notes that specialized attention patterns can have costly memory access and substantially larger actual latency than convolutional networks even when accuracy/FLOPs trade-offs appear competitive. Edge-oriented ViT work similarly treats inference latency and resource constraints as first-class problems, using model splitting or pruning rather than relying on parameter or FLOP counts. Consequently, an open practical problem is to compare ViT and CNN backbones under the same resolution, batch size, hardware, compiler, kernel implementation and serving budget. FLOPs, parameter count, throughput and wall-clock latency answer different questions, and one cannot be inferred from another. [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:11:8c6502676046:claim:2639c62fb151] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:a0fd92373ce7] [E:arxiv:2505.03113:abstract:claim:031cda985d75]

Representation differences create an open evaluation problem: ViTs and CNNs can be similarly accurate while behaving differently. CKA analysis finds that ViTs have more uniform representations across layers, preserve greater similarity between lower and higher layers, aggregate global information early through self-attention, and strongly propagate features through residual connections; ResNets instead show more separated lower- and higher-stage representations. Broader behavioral comparisons report differences in mistake types, calibration, transferability and feature invariance even when ImageNet accuracy and compute are similar. Thus, top-1 accuracy alone cannot determine robustness or suitability for a specialized task. The field still needs task-specific, distribution-shift and calibration evaluations that hold architecture, pretraining objective and data scale constant. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:6bd2853bda8d] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:7ba124bd8379] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:edef6a17e795] [E:arxiv:2311.09215:abstract:claim:06141737f41f] [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3]

Pretraining paradigm confounds many architecture comparisons. A ViT may be trained supervisedly, with CLIP, or with self-supervised methods such as DINO or MAE, while CNN backbones may use the same objectives but not realize identical representations. Battle of the Backbones separates architecture from pretraining method and dataset scale and reports that supervised convolutional models were strongest on most tasks among the models considered, while also noting that conclusions about self-supervised learning change in apples-to-apples comparisons at similar data scale. CLIP studies likewise find substantial architecture-dependent classification differences and normalization effects despite the same data and objective. An unresolved challenge is disentangling what comes from convolution or attention from what comes from the pretraining corpus, objective and augmentation; pooling all such results into one ViT-versus-CNN ranking is not valid. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:16b16c742158] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:d771ae86e0a5] [E:arxiv:2312.14400:abstract:claim:2ffa35fe91b3]

Hybrid and hierarchical Transformers demonstrate remedies but leave the original comparison less clean rather than resolving it. PVT, Swin, CvT, HVT and ViT-CoMer respectively add pyramid stages, windowed hierarchy, convolutional tokenization and projection, progressive pooling, or CNN–Transformer fusion. Their improvements support the value of locality, multi-scale features and sequence reduction, but each result is attributable to a modified architecture and often a different pretraining condition. The open problem is experimental attribution: future comparisons need ablations that add one property at a time—locality, hierarchy, windowing, positional treatment and pretraining—while keeping capacity, data and task heads fixed. Without those ablations, a hybrid model's AP, mIoU or ImageNet accuracy cannot be read as a direct verdict on the original ViT or on CNNs. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:17:b69e9ecbfb76:claim:5e1a7d1cbd79] [E:arxiv:2103.14030:section:abstract:17:c6cf3c9deb09:claim:4006dac09dbe] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:f6e0fad53ed7] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:178259056d55] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:1:697f0e7fca3b:claim:43e71b72c083]

Positional encoding and resolution transfer remain a practical design issue for plain Transformers. ViT adds positional information to patch embeddings, whereas CvT reports that its convolutional token embedding and convolutional projection allow explicit positional encoding to be removed, simplifying higher-resolution design. This points to a broader unresolved trade-off: explicit position embeddings encode token layout but may require adaptation when resolution or patch geometry changes, while convolutional structure supplies implicit spatial bias at the cost of the architecture's convolution-free purity. The source evidence supports this as a design concern addressed by CvT; it does not establish that every ViT positional scheme fails at resolution transfer or that convolutions are the only possible remedy. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1f5175d9cd68] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:34a85d41feb6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:3:156825dea060:claim:6755fdc45ff8]

Finally, task coverage remains uneven in the original ViT evidence. The original paper's strongest claims concern image-recognition transfer on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and related benchmarks, whereas dense-prediction evidence comes mainly from redesigned Transformer backbones or adapted ViTs. PVT's COCO RetinaNet gains and ViT-CoMer's detection and segmentation results show that Transformer-oriented backbones can be effective, but they do not establish that the original single-scale ViT has the same backbone utility. The concrete implication is that future work should report matched classification, detection, segmentation, OOD, calibration, latency and resolution-transfer results for the same initialization and training budget; until then, the defensible conclusion is conditional complementarity rather than a universal winner. ## Conclusion

The defensible answer is conditional complementarity rather than a universal winner. Under the original ViT paper’s large-data transfer regime, the plain patch Transformer was a strong classification competitor to CNNs; under smaller-data settings discussed by CvT and in broad Battle of the Backbones comparisons, ViTs showed greater sensitivity to pretraining-data amount and model capacity, while supervised convolutional models were strongest on most tasks in that benchmark suite. For dense prediction, the key trade-off is structural: CNNs and redesigned Transformers such as PVT expose staged multi-scale features, whereas the original ViT’s single-grid class-token design was not a ready CNN-style backbone. PVT’s COCO RetinaNet gains and ViT-CoMer’s enhanced detection and segmentation results support pyramid or convolutional adaptations, not retroactive superiority of original ViT. Efficiency likewise depends on resolution, hardware and metric, so matched classification, detection, segmentation, OOD, calibration and latency comparisons are required before choosing one family.
